title: The Day Boston Was Hit by a Molasses Tsunami

scenes.narration: A 15-foot wave once tore through Boston.
It wasn't water.
It was molasses.
On January 15, 1919, a massive storage tank stood in Boston's North End.
Inside were more than two million gallons of molasses.
Then, without warning, the tank burst apart.
Witnesses described a thunderous crash.
And suddenly, an enormous dark wave surged through the streets.
The wave was reportedly as high as 15 feet in places and moved fast enough to catch people completely off guard.
Buildings were smashed.
A section of the elevated railway was damaged.
Horses, carts, and people were swept into the chaos.
Twenty-one people were killed, and roughly 150 were injured.
But then rescuers discovered another problem.
Molasses is incredibly sticky.
As the syrup cooled, it became thicker, trapping debris and making rescue efforts extremely difficult.
Crews spent days cleaning the neighborhood.
Salt water from the harbor was reportedly used to help wash the molasses away.
Investigators eventually focused on the tank itself.
It had been built quickly, had reportedly leaked before the disaster, and was later found to have serious structural problems.
The company that owned it blamed sabotage.
But after years of legal battles, it was held responsible.
The event became known as the Great Molasses Flood.
And for decades afterward, some Boston residents claimed that on hot summer days...
you could still smell molasses in the neighborhood.
